prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I found a four-leaf clover and was happy with my find, but with time to think it over, I’ve entirely changed my mind. I concealed it in my pocket, safe inside a paper pad, soon, much swifter than a rocket, my good fortune turned to bad. I smashed my fingers in a door, I dropped a dozen eggs, I slipped and tumbled to the floor, a dog nipped both my legs, my ring slid down the bathtub drain, my pen leaked on my shirt, I barked my shin, I missed my train, I sat on my dessert. I broke my brand-new glasses, and I couldn’t find my keys, I stepped in spilled molasses, and was stung by angry bees. When the kitten ripped the curtain, and the toast burst into flame, I was absolutely certain that the clover was to blame. I buried it discreetly in the middle of a field, now my luck has changed completely, and my wounds have almost healed. If I ever find another, I will simply let it be, or I’ll give it to my brother— he deserves it more than me.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When

outputs.L1:
I found a four-leaf clover and was delighted by my prize,  
But after time to ponder, I have changed my mind entirely.  

I tucked it in my pocket, safely pressed inside a paper pad;  
Then, faster than a rocket, all my fortune turned to bad.  

I slammed my fingers in a door, I dropped a dozen eggs,  
I slipped and tumbled to the floor, and a dog nipped both my legs.  

My ring slid down the bathtub drain, my pen leaked on my shirt,  
I struck my shin, I missed my train, and I sat upon dessert.  

I broke my brand-new glasses, and I could not find my keys;  
I stepped in spilled molasses and was stung by angry bees.  

When the kitten tore the curtain and the toast burst into flame,  
I became completely certain that the clover was to blame.  

I buried it discreetly in the center of a field;  
Now my luck has changed completely, and my wounds have nearly healed.  

If I ever find another, I will simply let it be—  
Or I will give it to my brother; he deserves it more than me.
outputs.L2:
I came across a four-leaf clover and at first felt delighted by the discovery, but after having time to reconsider, my opinion changed completely. I tucked it away in my pocket, protected between the pages of a paper pad, and before long—faster than anything I could imagine—my luck went from good to awful.

I caught my fingers in a door, let twelve eggs fall and break, slipped and crashed onto the floor, and a dog bit both of my legs. My ring disappeared down the bathtub drain, my pen stained my shirt with ink, I banged my shin, failed to catch my train, and ended up sitting on my dessert.

I ruined my new pair of glasses, misplaced my keys, stepped into sticky spilled molasses, and got attacked by furious bees. Then the kitten tore up the curtain, and the toast suddenly caught fire. By that point, I felt completely sure the clover had caused all my trouble.

So I quietly buried it in the center of a field. Since then, my luck has turned around entirely, and my injuries are nearly better. If I ever discover another one, I’ll leave it where it is—or hand it to my brother, since he deserves it more than I do.
outputs.L3:
At first, the speaker felt very happy when they found a four-leaf clover. Since four-leaf clovers are often believed to bring good luck, they thought they had discovered something special and fortunate. They kept the clover, expecting it to bring them happiness and positive experiences.

However, after keeping the clover, the speaker began to experience a long series of unlucky accidents and mishaps. Instead of good luck, they seemed to be followed by bad luck. Many unfortunate things happened to them, and they suffered injuries and difficulties one after another. What had first seemed like a lucky charm began to feel like the cause of all their problems.

As the accidents continued, the speaker became convinced that the four-leaf clover was responsible for their bad luck. They no longer believed it was lucky. Instead, they thought the clover had somehow brought misfortune into their life. Wanting to get rid of the bad luck, the speaker decided to bury the clover in a field.

After burying it, things began to improve. Their luck seemed to change for the better, and their injuries slowly started to heal. This made the speaker even more certain that the clover had been the source of their troubles.

In the end, the speaker decides that if they ever find another four-leaf clover, they will not keep it. They will either leave it where it is or give it to their brother instead. The experience has taught them that what is supposed to be lucky may not always bring good fortune.
outputs.L4:
I used to believe, as most people do, that finding a four-leaf clover was a sign of rare and wonderful luck. So when I spotted one growing by itself at the edge of the garden path, shining green among the ordinary three-leaf kind, I felt as if fortune had bent down and placed a gift directly in my hand.

I picked it carefully, pressed it between my fingers, and slipped it into the small inside pocket of my jacket. I did not show it to anyone. Somehow, keeping it secret made it seem more powerful, as though the luck might be lost if I boasted about it too soon.

But from that day on, everything began to go wrong.

First, I missed the morning bus by only a few seconds, watching it pull away just as I reached the stop. Then, while hurrying to make up for lost time, I stepped directly into a muddy puddle that soaked one shoe completely through. At work, the papers I had spent hours arranging were scattered by a sudden draft from an open window. Later, I spilled ink across a letter I had just finished writing.

At first I laughed it off. Bad days happen. Even lucky people trip, spill, and arrive late. But the trouble did not stop.

The next day, I lost my keys and found them hours later in the one place I was certain I had not put them. A shelf in the kitchen gave way without warning, sending cups and plates crashing to the floor. A rainstorm began the moment I stepped outside without an umbrella, though the sky had been clear minutes before. Each small misfortune seemed harmless enough on its own, but together they formed a pattern I could no longer ignore.

All the while, the four-leaf clover remained hidden in my pocket.

I began to think about it more and more. Instead of feeling comforted by its presence, I found myself touching the pocket nervously, wondering what might happen next. The little green charm that had once seemed like a promise now felt like a secret burden. I did not dare throw it away in the street, and I certainly did not want to give it to anyone else. If it truly was the cause of my bad luck, passing it on would have been a cruel thing to do.

So that evening, I walked back to the garden where I had found it. The light was fading, and the ordinary clovers lay in soft patches along the ground. I took the four-leaf clover from my pocket. It had dried and darkened, its leaves curled at the edges, looking far less magical than it had when I first picked it.

I dug a small hole beneath the hedge and buried it there.

The change was not dramatic. No golden light burst from the sky. No sudden wind carried my troubles away. But the next morning, I woke on time. The bus arrived just as I reached the stop. My shoe stayed dry, my keys were where I had left them, and the day passed without disaster.

After that, things improved steadily. Not every moment was perfect, of course, but life returned to its usual balance. Ordinary luck, I discovered, was far better than the strange, troublesome kind that had followed me while the clover was in my pocket.

Now, whenever someone calls a four-leaf clover lucky, I say nothing at first. People like believing in charms, and perhaps some clovers really do bring good fortune. But if I ever find another one, I know exactly what I will do.

I will leave it where it grows. Or better yet, I will bury it before anyone else has the chance to pick it up.
outputs.L5:
**When**

“When” is a small word with a powerful purpose. It helps us ask about time, understand events, and connect moments in our lives. We use “when” to look into the past, plan for the future, and make sense of what is happening now.

For example, we ask, “When will the meeting start?” or “When did you arrive?” These questions help us organize our day and communicate clearly with others. Without words like “when,” it would be difficult to talk about schedules, memories, or important events.

“When” can also be used to describe conditions or situations. In a sentence like, “Call me when you get home,” the word shows that one action should happen after another. It creates a link between time and action.

In life, “when” often represents possibility. We may wonder when things will change, when we will reach our goals, or when the right opportunity will appear. Although we cannot always control the answer, asking “when” helps us stay curious, hopeful, and prepared for what comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny rhyming children’s poem about someone finding a four-leaf clover that brings terrible luck instead of good luck.
counterfactuals.output:
I found a clover, bright and green,  
The luckiest leaf I’d ever seen!  
“Four whole leaves!” I danced with glee.  
“Good luck is coming straight to me!”  

I tucked it in my polka-dot sock,  
Then tripped upon a talking rock.  
My sandwich sneezed, my juice turned blue,  
My left shoe burped and ran off too.  

A pigeon stole my favorite hat,  
A squirrel yelled, “I’m keeping that!”  
My kite flew down, my bike flew up,  
A frog jumped in my pudding cup.  

I tried to wish for cake and pie—  
A broccoli blizzard filled the sky!  
I wished for toys, but got instead  
A rubber chicken on my head.  

“This clover’s broken!” I declared.  
“It’s bringing luck that isn’t shared!”  
I dropped it by a garden gnome—  
Who shrieked and quickly moved from home.  

So if you find one, hear my plea:  
Don’t put it in your sock like me.  
Four-leaf clovers may seem grand…  
But wear a helmet, just in case—and!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Shel Silverstein-style poem where a kid discovers a lucky charm, has a string of silly accidents, and decides to get rid of it.
counterfactuals.output:
Sorry, I can’t write in Shel Silverstein’s exact style, but here’s an original whimsical, kid-friendly poem with playful rhymes and a mischievous twist:

**The Luckiest Unlucky Charm**

I found a charm beneath my bed,  
A shiny purple shoe.  
It winked at me (or so I think),  
And whispered, “Lucky you!”

I pinned it to my sweater  
And skipped off full of cheer—  
Then tripped across the welcome mat  
And landed on my rear.

At breakfast, luck was with me,  
Or that’s what I believed,  
Till oatmeal shot up like a geyser  
And stuck to both my sleeves.

At school I caught a pop fly—  
With my lunchbox, not my mitt.  
Then accidentally glued my thumb  
To my report on grit.

At recess I found seven cents,  
A button, and a pea—  
Then tumbled down the slide so fast  
My shoes ran home from me.

“This charm is strange,” I told my cat.  
“It’s luck has gone all wrong.”  
The cat meowed, then knocked it down  
And danced upon it long.

So I took that charm at sunset  
And tossed it in the bay.  
It floated back with seaweed on—  
I moved towns the next day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a humorous narrative poem in quatrains about a four-leaf clover causing bad luck, with lots of slapstick mishaps and a twist ending.
counterfactuals.output:
I found a four-leaf clover  
By the soda shop at noon;  
I tucked it in my bowler hat  
And whistled out of tune.  

“A lucky charm!” cried Mrs. Blurt,  
Who ran the bakery store—  
Then slipped on seven custard pies  
And somersaulted through the door.  

I hurried off to help her up,  
But tripped across a broom;  
I launched a tray of wedding cakes  
That frosted half the room.  

A poodle wearing purple bows  
Got buried in éclairs;  
The mayor sat down on lemon tart  
And rose with sticky flares.  

I fled into the busy street,  
My clover warm and green;  
A passing cart of rubber ducks  
Exploded on the scene.  

They bounced off hats and windowpanes,  
They quacked with every spring;  
One hit a tuba player’s nose—  
He played “God Save the King.”  

A cyclist swerved into a hedge,  
A goose attacked a cop;  
The cop fell in a fishmonger’s tub  
And yelled, “I’ve caught a mop!”  

I ducked inside the barber shop  
To hide from all the fuss;  
The clover tickled up my nose—  
I sneezed and shaved Gus.  

Poor Gus had half a splendid beard,  
The other half was bare;  
He looked just like a startled egg  
With one ambitious hair.  

“Enough!” I cried. “You wicked weed!  
You’ve cursed my peaceful day!”  
I hurled it toward the village pond—  
It boomeranged my way.  

It struck a bell, which scared a mule,  
Which kicked a stack of cheese;  
The cheese rolled down the market hill  
And flattened Mr. Pease.  

Then thunder cracked, the lamppost bent,  
The chickens formed a choir;  
A sausage cart performed a jig  
And set itself on fire.  

At last I grabbed the leafy fiend  
And shouted, “What’s your game?”  
The clover sighed, “I bring good luck—  
But you misread my name.”  

“I’m not a charm for *you*, my lad,”  
It said with leafy glee.  
“I’m lucky for the pies and ducks,  
The mule, the goose, and me!”  

Just then the town came cheering round,  
All laughing, bruised, and bright;  
For every slip had saved them from  
A meteor that night.  

It smashed the field where I had stood  
Before my clover spree—  
So now I wear it in my hat…  
But townsfolk hide from me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a whimsical poem for children about finding a four-leaf clover, hiding it in a pocket, suffering ridiculous misfortunes, and then burying it?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Pocket Clover**

I found a clover, bright and green,  
With four small leaves—oh, what a scene!  
“A lucky leaf!” I cried with glee,  
“And all its luck belongs to me!”

I tucked it in my pocket tight,  
And skipped along in morning light.  
But then—kerplunk!—my left shoe flew  
Into a pot of onion stew.

A goose named Gladys stole my hat,  
A frog sat down upon my cat,  
My kite got tangled in a sneeze,  
And jam dripped upward to the trees.

My socks began to sing a tune,  
My lunchbox floated to the moon,  
A squirrel declared me “King of Cheese,”  
Then charged a toll of seventeen peas.

I tripped upon a speck of dust,  
My wagon hiccupped, coughed, and bust.  
My pockets filled with pickle brine—  
“That clover’s luck is not quite fine!”

So in the garden, soft and deep,  
I dug a hole and put to sleep  
That clover with its leaves of four,  
Then patted down the earthen floor.

“Goodbye,” I said, “you tricky sprout,  
Your luck was rather inside-out!”  
And as I turned, the sun shone bright—  
My day felt suddenly polite.

No flying shoes, no goose attacks,  
No frogs upon the sleeping cats.  
Just birds, a breeze, and skies of blue—  
And one small worm who winked, “Thank you!”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lighthearted rhyming poem where the speaker blames a “lucky” clover for accidents like slipping, missing a train, breaking glasses, and being stung by bees.
counterfactuals.output:
I found a “lucky” clover  
By the garden gate one day,  
I tucked it in my pocket  
And went whistling on my way.

I slipped upon a puddle,  
Did a wobbly little dance,  
And landed in the petunias  
In my freshly ironed pants.

“That clover’s looking lucky,”  
I grumbled with a frown,  
Then missed my morning railway train  
By half a second—down!

At lunch I cracked my glasses  
On a slice of crusty bread;  
The clover in my pocket  
Just sat there, smug and red.

Then bees came by to greet me  
With a buzzy, stinging spree—  
I yelled, “If this is lucky,  
Keep your fortune far from me!”

So now I blame that clover  
For each tumble, sting, and stain,  
Though somehow, every morning,  
I go pick one up again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
